newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich ethics woes not a big concern at home.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich ethics woes not a big concern at home.

text.p: While the House grapples with whether to re-elect Newt Gingrich as speaker, constituents in his congressional district say they are unconcerned by claims of ethics violations that many of them view as politically motivated.

Gingrich's admission that he gave inaccurate information to a House ethics subcommittee about the role of a political action committee in a college course he taught has caused far greater controversy in the nation's capital than in his conservative Republican district in suburban Atlanta.
"They're just making a mountain out of a molehill," Dorothy Herchelroth, 84, of Marietta said. "They've sworn for years to make him an awful person. And he isn't."
Barry Brown, a data centre supervisor who described himself as a moderate, said he believes the ethics committee probe is "politics as usual."
"If there is any substance at all, then obviously he should step down. But I don't think that's the case. I think it's much ado about nothing," Brown said.

After a re-election campaign in which Gingrich defeated millionaire cookie magnate Michael Coles two months ago, supporters view the ethics issue as spurious, while critics have added it to their already lengthy list of complaints about the speaker's style of government. Gingrich staffers say they have seen no change in his popularity.

"Newt still has tremendous support here," Gingrich spokesman Allan Lipsett said. "The calls that we've been getting here in the district office have been running 100-to-1 in support of him. People here expect him to be re-elected speaker."
Republican Congressman Bob Barr, who won election in an adjacent district during the 1994 Republican revolution, said Georgians are tired of people "consumed with hatred for Newt."
"My constituents are telling me they don't want to concentrate on individual and personal attacks on people. We want you to balance the budget," Barr said.

Gingrich's 6th Congressional District is mostly white and conservative. "They'll give you anything, but if you try to take it away from them, they'll kill you," is the way one resident described his neighbours.
Ethics has repeatedly been raised as an issue against Gingrich, a Georgia congressman since 1978. But it has not prevented him from consistently winning re-election.

Questions over the financing of the course Gingrich taught at Kennesaw State University and Reinhardt College are not new to Georgians, having been disclosed in reports in the Atlanta Journal-Constitution newspaper in 1993.
Gingrich admitted Dec. 21 that he violated House rules by not getting legal advise about political aspects of the tax-exempt college courses.
One restaurant owner, though, said he was not paying much attention to the dispute because he felt the ethics committee was "an O.J. jury" likely to clear Gingrich of any wrongdoing.
